cards.title: 2.1 The Middle East
body: Identify the European colonial powers in the Middle East.
France had a long history of commercial and cultural associations in the Levant (eastern Mediterranean countries).
French commercial interest dates back to the 16th century.
By the end of the eighteenth century France’s Levantine trade was three times that of England.
After the First World War, greater Syria became a French mandate.

cards.title: Middle East
body: After the war: end of European mandates, creation of Israel (1948) and repeated Arab–Israeli wars, oil as a strategic prize, Nasser’s Egypt as a non-aligned leader, later Iranian revolution and Gulf conflicts. Superpowers fish in every crisis.

cards.title: Camp David: the first Arab–Israeli peace treaty
body: **Step 1 – the wars before.** After the 1967 war Israel occupied Arab land, and in 1973 Egypt led a new attack on Israel. A UN-negotiated cease-fire ended that war in 1974.
**Step 2 – US pressure.** In 1977 US President **Jimmy Carter** began pressing for a compromise peace.

**Step 3 – the meeting.** In **September 1978** Carter met Egypt's President **Anwar Sadat** and Israel's Prime Minister **Menachem Begin** at **Camp David** (USA). The result was the **Camp David Accords**.

**Step 4 – the treaty.** In **March 1979** Sadat and Begin signed an Israeli–Egyptian peace treaty that ended the state of war between them. **Egypt** thus became the first Arab country to recognize Israel.
**Step 5 – the limit.** Many Arab countries continued to refuse to recognize Israel.
**Memory trick:** "Carter + Sadat + Begin = Camp David (1978), treaty 1979."
**Exam tip:** "The only/first Arab country to recognize Israel" (in this course) = Egypt.

cards.title: Past exam (Matric 2026)
cards.q: Identify the **wrong** pairing in relation to European occupation in Middle East.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** From the lesson: “After the First World War, greater Syria became a French mandate (Lebanon and Syria under France; Iraq under Britain).”

**Step 2:** **Yemen** (specifically the port of Aden) was under **British** influence/control, not French. Lebanon and Syria were French mandates after WWI.

**Step 3:** So the answer is A) Yemen -------------------- France.

cards.title: Model answer: the Middle East after 1945
cards.problem: (Exam question) Describe the main developments in the Middle East after the Second World War.

steps.text: Background: Britain and France held the region – greater Syria became a French mandate after the First World War, with France's trade links in the Levant dating back to the 16th century.
End of mandates: European mandates ended after 1945.
Israel: the state of Israel was created in 1948, followed by repeated Arab–Israeli wars (e.g. the Six-Day War 1967).
Other themes: oil as a strategic prize, Nasser's Egypt as a non-aligned leader, the Iranian revolution and the Gulf conflicts – with the superpowers involved in every crisis.

cards.answer: The end of British and French mandates, the creation of Israel (1948) and Arab–Israeli wars, the strategic value of oil, Nasser's non-aligned Egypt and later the Iranian revolution and Gulf wars – all shaped by Cold War rivalry.

cards.title: 2.2 China and Japan
body: By 1945, there were two Chinese governments.
The Nationalist government of Chiang Kai-shek, based in southern and central China, was supported by the United States.
The Communist government, under the leadership of Mao Zedong, had its base in North China.
In 1946, full-scale civil war between the Nationalists and the Communists broke out.
In the countryside, millions of peasants were attracted to the Communists by promises of land.

cards.title: China and Japan
body: **China:** 1949 Communist victory (Mao). Later split with the USSR, UN seat moves to Beijing, Deng’s reforms after Mao. **Japan:** US occupation, new constitution, then economic miracle as a US ally in Asia.

cards.title: Deng Xiaoping and the Four Modernizations
body: **Step 1 – the end of the Mao era.** Mao Zedong died in **September 1976**. A group of reformers led by **Deng Xiaoping** took power and ended the Cultural Revolution.
**Step 2 – the policy.** Deng followed the **Four Modernizations**, focusing on four areas: **industry, agriculture, technology and national defence**.

**Step 3 – opening up.** China had been cut off from world technology for over 20 years, so the government invited **foreign investors** and sent thousands of students abroad to study science and technology.
**Step 4 – result.** China's economy grew fast, but the Communist Party kept political control (as the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown later showed).
**Memory trick – "I-A-T-D":** Industry, Agriculture, Technology, Defence.
**Exam tip:** Mao = Great Leap Forward and Cultural Revolution; Deng = Four Modernizations. Do not mix up the leaders.

**Step 3:** **Mao Ze Dong** led the Communist Party of China (CPC) to victory in 1949.

cards.why:
**Step 1:** From the lesson: “China: 1949 Communist victory (Mao).”

**Step 2:** The **Great Leap Forward** (1958–1962) was an economic and social campaign by the Communist Party of China aimed at rapidly transforming the country from an agrarian economy into a socialist society through rapid industrialization and collectivization.

**Step 3:** So the answer is B) Great Leap Forward.

**Step 2:** Japan invaded Manchuria (a northern province of China) in 1931 and set up a puppet state called Manchukuo, an event often seen as a precursor to WWII in Asia.

**Step 3:** So the answer is D) Manchuria..

cards.title: Model answer: the Chinese Civil War
cards.problem: (Exam question) Why did the Communists win the Chinese Civil War?

steps.text: Two governments by 1945: the Nationalists of Chiang Kai-shek in southern and central China (supported by the USA) and the Communists of Mao Zedong based in North China.
Full-scale civil war broke out in 1946.
Peasant support: in the countryside millions of peasants were attracted to the Communists by promises of land.
Result: Communist victory in 1949; later China split with the USSR, took the UN seat and reformed under Deng after Mao.

cards.answer: Mao's Communists won (1949) mainly because promises of land won over millions of peasants, while the US-backed Nationalists of Chiang Kai-shek lost popular support.

lessons.title: Decolonization and Independent states in South and Southeast Asia

cards.title: 2.3 Decolonization and Independent states in South and Southeast Asia
body: At the end of World War II, British India’s Muslims and Hindus were bitterly divided.
The British decided to divide India into two countries, one majority Hindu (India) and the other Muslim (Pakistan).
Pakistan consisted of two regions separated by India.
One part, West Pakistan, was to the northwest of India.
On August 15, 1947, India and Pakistan became independent.

cards.title: South & Southeast Asia
body: Britain leaves India (1947) — partition into India and Pakistan. Other colonies follow: Burma, Ceylon, Indonesia (from the Dutch), Indochina after Dien Bien Phu and then Vietnam’s long war. Paths differ: some negotiated, some fought.

cards.title: Exam habit
body: Always name the colonial power, the year, and whether independence was negotiated or armed. “Asia decolonised” is too vague.

cards.title: Unit 2 summary in full – the Middle East and Asia after 1945
body: **Point 1 – colonial background.** Most of the Middle East and Asia had been colonized by European powers. Japan, the only Asian imperialist power, invaded most of Asia during the Second World War.
**Point 2 – a wave of new states.** With the end of the Second World War many newly independent nations appeared in the Middle East and Asia.

**Point 3 – the Arab states.** Nationalist movements won independence for **Syria and Lebanon in 1946**. **Iraq** was declared independent in **1932** but remained under British control even after independence. **South Yemen** was liberated by nationalist liberation movements in **1967**. The small Arab Gulf states became independent one after another.
**Point 4 – South Asia.** British South Asia was divided into **India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka and later Bangladesh**.
**Point 5 – Southeast Asia.** Wars of liberation produced the independent states of **Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia**, among others.
**Key terms to know:** Cultural Revolution, commune, Great Leap Forward, Intifada, occupation, state capitalism.
**Memory trick – the key dates "32-46-67":** Iraq 1932, Syria and Lebanon 1946, South Yemen 1967.
**Exam tip:** The true/false items in this unit change these dates (e.g. "Syria and Lebanon 1992", "South Yemen 1905") – learn the three dates and the false ones are easy to spot.

cards.title: Past exam (Matric 2017)
cards.q: One of the following **was not** a British colony in Asia.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** From the lesson: “Other colonies follow: Burma, Ceylon, Indonesia (from the Dutch), Indochina after Dien Bien Phu and then Vietnam’s long war.”

**Step 2:** Indonesia was a colony of the Netherlands (Dutch East Indies), not Britain. Ceylon (Sri Lanka), Pakistan, India, and Burma were all part of the British Empire.

**Step 3:** So the answer is C) Indonesia.

**Tip:** Underline the key word in the question (true / not / except / first / last), then test every option against the lesson facts and dates.

cards.title: Past exam (Matric 2018)
cards.q: The US colony in Southeast Asia was ...
cards.why:
**Step 1:** From the lesson: “Always name the colonial power, the year, and whether independence was negotiated or armed (the Philippines was a US colony).”

**Step 2:** The **Philippines** became a US colony following the Spanish-American War in 1898. It remained under US control until it gained independence in 1946.

**Step 3:** So the answer is A) the Philippines..

**Tip:** Underline the key word in the question (true / not / except / first / last), then test every option against the lesson facts and dates.

cards.title: Past exam (Matric 2020)
cards.q: Which country remained as an independent buffer state between the French and the British colonies in South East Asia?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** From the lesson: “Paths differ: some negotiated, some fought (Thailand stayed independent between British and French colonies).”

**Step 2:** Thailand (then known as Siam) was the only country in Southeast Asia that was never colonized by European powers. It served as a 'buffer state' between British-controlled Burma/Malaya and French-controlled Indochina.

**Step 3:** So the answer is C) Thailand.

**Tip:** Underline the key word in the question (true / not / except / first / last), then test every option against the lesson facts and dates.

cards.title: Model answer: independence of India
cards.problem: (Exam question) How did India gain independence, and why was it divided?

steps.text: Name the power and year: Britain left India in 1947.
Why divided: at the end of World War II British India's Muslims and Hindus were bitterly divided.
The solution: Britain divided India into a mainly Hindu India and a Muslim Pakistan (two regions, West and East, separated by India).
Date: India and Pakistan became independent on 15 August 1947 – a negotiated path.

cards.answer: Britain granted independence by negotiation on 15 August 1947, partitioning British India into India (mainly Hindu) and Pakistan (Muslim) because of Hindu–Muslim division.

questions.q: The Arab - Israel conflict of 1967 was also known as **______**.
questions.label: 9. The Arab - Israel conflict of 1967 was also known as **______**.
why: Answer C: Six days war

From the lesson: “After the war: end of European mandates, creation of Israel (1948) and repeated Arab–Israeli wars, oil as a strategic prize, Nasser’s Egypt as a non-aligned leader, later Iranian revolution and Gulf conflicts.”
The 1967 conflict between Israel and its Arab neighbors (Egypt, Jordan, and Syria) is known as the **Six-Day War** because it lasted from June 5 to June 10, 1967.
So the answer is C) Six days war.

questions.q: The Nationalist party in China was led by **______**.
questions.label: 11. The Nationalist party in China was led by **______**.
why: Answer E: None

The Nationalist Party of China (Kuomintang or KMT) was led by **Sun Yat-sen** and later, most famously, by **Chiang Kai-shek**. 
- Mao Zedong (A) led the Communist Party.
- Deng Xiaoping (C) was a later Communist leader.
- Xi Jinping (D) is the current Communist leader.
Since Chiang Kai-shek is not listed, 'None' is the correct choice.
So the answer is E) None.

questions.q: Which one of the following was not **French Indochina** colony?
questions.label: 12. Which one of the following was not **French Indochina** colony?
why: Answer A: Thailand

French Indochina consisted of Vietnam, Cambodia, and Laos. **Thailand** (then known as Siam) managed to remain independent and served as a 'buffer state' between French and British colonial territories in Southeast Asia.
So the answer is A) Thailand.

questions.q: All of the following were colonial powers of Southeast Asia, **except**
questions.label: 13. All of the following were colonial powers of Southeast Asia, **except**
why: Answer E: None

**Analysis:** All the countries listed were colonial powers in Southeast Asia. 
- **Great Britain** ruled Burma and Malaya. 
- **Portugal** ruled East Timor. 
- **USA** ruled the Philippines. 
- **France** ruled Indochina (Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia). 
Since all are colonial powers, none of the options A-D is an exception.
So the answer is E) None.
